method_card.title: Transformers and Electromagnetic Induction
steps: Pick the equation: turns ratio for voltage or turns, power balance (Vp Ip = Vs Is) for current.
Rearrange for the unknown, then substitute the values.
Two-step questions: find the missing voltage or current first.
State the answer with its unit (V, A, %, or W).
method_card.content:
Two equations solve almost every transformer question.

  • Turns ratio: \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\). More secondary turns steps the voltage up (current down); fewer steps it down.
  • Power balance for a 100% efficient transformer: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\). Use it for current questions.

The National Grid transmits at very high voltage so the current is small. Power lost as heat in cables is \(I^2R\), and because current is squared, a small current means far less waste.

exam_context.frequency: High. Transformers appear on almost every Paper 2

gold.display: A power station generates 25 MW at 25,000 V. A step-up transformer increases the voltage to 400,000 V. The cables have a total resistance of 10 Ω. Calculate the power lost in the cables at 400,000 V. Give your answer to 1 decimal place in kW.

misconceptions.message: First find current: I = P/V = 25,000,000/400,000 = 62.5 A. Then loss = I²R = 62.5² × 10 = 39,062.5 W = 39.1 kW.
Power loss = I²R. Don't forget to square the current: 62.5² = 3906.25.

gold.hint: Find the current with I = P ÷ V, then loss = I² R; remember to square the current.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: find the current at the transmission voltage, then the heating loss \(= I^2 R\). Work in base units first.

guided_steps.hint: Divide power by voltage.

guided_steps.say: The current is squared: this is the whole reason high voltage helps.
guided_steps.hint: Square the current before multiplying by resistance.
Multiply by the cable resistance.
Divide watts by 1000; keep the exact value for now.
guided_steps.done: Rounded to 1 decimal place, the power lost is 39.1 kW.

gold.display: A power station generates 25 MW at 25,000 V. The cables have a resistance of 10 Ω. Calculate the power lost in the cables if the electricity is transmitted at 25,000 V (without a step-up transformer). Give your answer in MW.

misconceptions.message: At 25 kV: I = P/V = 25,000,000/25,000 = 1000 A. Loss = I²R = 1000² × 10 = 10,000,000 W = 10 MW. That's 40% of total power wasted!
Power loss = I²R. Current is SQUARED: this is why high currents waste so much energy.

gold.hint: Same steps as the step-up case but with the full 1000 A current.

guided_steps.say: Same method with no step-up transformer: find the current, then loss \(= I^2 R\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide power by voltage.

guided_steps.say: Ten times the current of the step-up case, and it is squared.
guided_steps.hint: Square the current first.
Multiply by the cable resistance.
Divide watts by 1,000,000.
guided_steps.done: 10 MW lost out of 25 MW, about 40% wasted, so the answer is 10 MW.

gold.display: A transformer steps down 240 V to 12 V. The secondary current is 4 A and the primary current is 0.25 A. Calculate the efficiency of the transformer as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Power out = 12 × 4 = 48 W. Power in = 240 × 0.25 = 60 W. Efficiency = (48/60) × 100 = 80%.
Efficiency = output ÷ input × 100. Output power (48 W) is always less than input (60 W).

guided_steps.say: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{power out}}{\text{power in}} \times 100\).

guided_steps.hint: Secondary voltage times secondary current.
Primary voltage times primary current.

guided_steps.say: That is the fraction; now turn it into a percentage.
guided_steps.hint: Divide output power by input power.
Multiply the fraction by 100.
guided_steps.done: 80% efficient: 48 W out of 60 W in, so the answer is 80%.

gold.display: A transformer needs to produce 9 V from a 230 V mains supply. If the secondary coil has 36 turns, how many primary turns are needed?

misconceptions.message: Step-down: primary needs MORE turns. np/ns = Vp/Vs = 230/9.

gold.hint: np = ns × Vp ÷ Vs; a big step-down needs more primary turns.

guided_steps.say: Turns ratio \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\), rearranged for the primary turns: \(n_p = n_s \times \frac{V_p}{V_s}\).

guided_steps.pre: Top of the fraction first: ns × Vp = 36 × 230 =
guided_steps.hint: Secondary turns times primary voltage.

guided_steps.say: A big step-down needs far more turns on the primary side.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the secondary voltage.
Multiply your answer by the secondary voltage.
guided_steps.done: Equals ns × Vp = 8280, so np = 920 turns.

gold.display: A power station generates electricity at 25,000 V. A step-up transformer with 500 primary turns increases this to 400,000 V. Calculate the number of secondary turns.

misconceptions.message: Step-up: more secondary turns. The ratio is 400,000/25,000 = 16.

guided_steps.say: \(n_s = n_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the secondary voltage by the primary voltage.

guided_steps.say: Step-up: many more turns on the secondary.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary turns by the voltage ratio.
Divide your answer by the primary turns.
guided_steps.done: Equals the voltage ratio 16, so ns = 8000 turns.

gold.display: A transformer is 90% efficient. The primary voltage is 230 V and the primary current is 2 A. The secondary voltage is 20 V. Calculate the secondary current. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Input power = 230 × 2 = 460 W. Output power = 460 × 0.9 = 414 W. Is = 414 ÷ 20 = 20.7 A.
Don't assume 100% efficiency. Output power = input power × efficiency = 460 × 0.9 = 414 W.

gold.hint: Power out = power in × 0.9, then Is = power out ÷ Vs.

guided_steps.say: Not 100% efficient, so power out = power in × efficiency, then \(I_s = \frac{\text{power out}}{V_s}\).

guided_steps.hint: Primary voltage times primary current.
Multiply by the efficiency as a decimal (0.9).

guided_steps.say: Lower secondary voltage, so a larger secondary current.
guided_steps.hint: Divide output power by the secondary voltage.
Multiply the secondary voltage by your answer.
guided_steps.done: Equals the output power 414 W, so Is = 20.7 A.

bronze.display: A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.
bronze.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns fraction ns over np.

guided_steps.say: Turns ratio: \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\). Rearranged for the secondary voltage: \(V_s = V_p \times \frac{n_s}{n_p}\).

guided_steps.pre: First the turns fraction, ns ÷ np = 50 ÷ 1000 =
guided_steps.hint: Divide the secondary turns by the primary turns.

guided_steps.say: Fewer secondary turns, so the voltage steps down.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns fraction.
Divide your answer by 230; it should return the turns fraction.
guided_steps.done: That matches the turns fraction 0.05, so Vs = 11.5 V.

bronze.display: A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 12 V. The primary coil has 460 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns.
bronze.hint: Rearrange to ns = np × Vs ÷ Vp, then work it out.

guided_steps.say: \(V_s = V_p \times \frac{n_s}{n_p}\), and here we want ns, so \(n_s = n_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}\).

guided_steps.pre: Top of the fraction first: np × Vs = 460 × 12 =
guided_steps.hint: Multiply primary turns by secondary voltage.

guided_steps.say: That is the number of secondary turns.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the primary voltage.
Multiply your answer by the primary voltage.
guided_steps.done: Equals np × Vs = 5520, so ns = 24 turns.

bronze.display: A transformer has 500 primary turns and 2000 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 25 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

misconceptions.message: Vs = 25 × (2000/500) = 25 × 4 = 100 V. More secondary turns = higher voltage (step-up).

bronze.hint: More secondary turns, so multiply Vp by the turns ratio ns over np.

guided_steps.say: \(V_s = V_p \times \frac{n_s}{n_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the secondary turns by the primary turns.

guided_steps.say: More secondary turns, so this is a step-up: the voltage rises.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns fraction.
Divide your answer by 25.
guided_steps.done: Matches the turns ratio 4, so Vs = 100 V.

bronze.display: A transformer has 1200 primary turns and 60 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 240 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

misconceptions.message: Vs = 240 × (60/1200) = 240 × 0.05 = 12 V. Fewer secondary turns = lower voltage (step-down).

bronze.hint: Multiply Vp by ns ÷ np; fewer secondary turns means a smaller voltage.

guided_steps.say: \(V_s = V_p \times \frac{n_s}{n_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the secondary turns by the primary turns.

guided_steps.say: Fewer secondary turns, so step-down: the voltage falls.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns fraction.
Divide your answer by 240.
guided_steps.done: Matches the turns fraction 0.05, so Vs = 12 V.

bronze.display: A transformer has 400 primary turns. The primary voltage is 230 V and the secondary voltage is 11.5 V. How many secondary turns does it have?
bronze.hint: Rearrange to ns = np × Vs ÷ Vp.

guided_steps.say: \(n_s = n_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}\).

guided_steps.pre: Top of the fraction first: np × Vs = 400 × 11.5 =
guided_steps.hint: Multiply primary turns by secondary voltage.

guided_steps.say: That is the number of secondary turns.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the primary voltage.
Multiply your answer by the primary voltage.
guided_steps.done: Equals np × Vs = 4600, so ns = 20 turns.

bronze.display: A transformer has 200 primary turns and 800 secondary turns. Is it a step-up or a step-down transformer?

misconceptions.message: More secondary turns (800) than primary (200) means the voltage is stepped UP. This is a step-up transformer.

bronze.display: A transformer has 600 primary turns and 300 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 120 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.
bronze.hint: Halve the primary voltage: the turns ratio is 300 over 600.

guided_steps.say: \(V_s = V_p \times \frac{n_s}{n_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the secondary turns by the primary turns.

guided_steps.say: Half the turns, so half the voltage.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns fraction.
Divide your answer by 120.
guided_steps.done: Matches the turns fraction 0.5, so Vs = 60 V.

bronze.display: A transformer has 4000 primary turns and 200 secondary turns. Is it a step-up or a step-down transformer?

misconceptions.message: Fewer secondary turns (200) than primary (4000) means the voltage is stepped DOWN. This is a step-down transformer.

silver.display: A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 11.5 V. The secondary current is 4 A. Calculate the primary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

misconceptions.message: Step-down transformer: lower voltage on secondary means HIGHER current. Ip < Is.

silver.hint: Use Vp Ip = Vs Is, then divide Vs Is by Vp.

guided_steps.say: Power in = power out for a 100% efficient transformer: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\). Rearranged: \(I_p = \frac{V_s I_s}{V_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply secondary voltage by secondary current.

guided_steps.say: Low-voltage side carries the higher current, so the primary current is small.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the primary voltage.
Multiply your answer by the primary voltage.
guided_steps.done: Equals Vs Is = 46, so Ip = 0.2 A.

silver.display: A step-up transformer has 500 primary turns and 10,000 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 25 V and the primary current is 20 A. Calculate the secondary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

misconceptions.message: Step-up increases voltage but decreases current. Is = 1 A, not 400 A.

silver.hint: Find Vs from the turns ratio first, then use power in = power out.

guided_steps.say: Two moves: the turns ratio gives Vs, then power balance gives Is.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns ratio.

guided_steps.say: That is the power passing through, in watts.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply primary voltage by primary current.
Divide the power by the secondary voltage.
Multiply secondary voltage by your answer.
guided_steps.done: Equals the input power 500 W, so Is = 1 A.

silver.display: A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V, primary current 0.5 A, and secondary voltage of 23 V. Calculate the secondary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

guided_steps.say: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\), so \(I_s = \frac{V_p I_p}{V_s}\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply primary voltage by primary current.

guided_steps.say: Lower secondary voltage, so a bigger secondary current.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the secondary voltage.
Multiply the secondary voltage by your answer.
guided_steps.done: Equals Vp Ip = 115, so Is = 5 A.

silver.display: A transformer steps down from 11,000 V to 220 V. The primary coil has 5000 turns. Calculate the number of secondary turns.

guided_steps.say: \(n_s = n_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the secondary voltage by the primary voltage.

guided_steps.say: Far fewer turns on the secondary: a big step-down.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the primary turns by the voltage fraction.
Divide primary turns by your answer.
guided_steps.done: Equals the voltage ratio 11,000 ÷ 220 = 50, so ns = 100 turns.

silver.display: A transformer steps down from 11,000 V to 220 V. The secondary current is 40 A. Calculate the primary current (assuming 100% efficiency).

misconceptions.message: Step-down: lower V means higher I on secondary. Primary current is much smaller.

guided_steps.say: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\), so \(I_p = \frac{V_s I_s}{V_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply secondary voltage by secondary current.

guided_steps.say: Step-down: low voltage means high current on the secondary, so the primary current is small.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the primary voltage.
Multiply the primary voltage by your answer.
guided_steps.done: Equals Vs Is = 8800, so Ip = 0.8 A.

silver.display: A charger has a secondary voltage of 6 V and secondary current of 2 A. The primary current is 0.1 A. Calculate the primary voltage (assuming 100% efficiency).

guided_steps.say: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\), so \(V_p = \frac{V_s I_s}{I_p}\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply secondary voltage by secondary current.

guided_steps.say: Tiny primary current, so a large primary voltage.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the primary current.
Multiply your answer by the primary current.
guided_steps.done: Equals Vs Is = 12, so Vp = 120 V.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, all values already in the right units: substitute and solve.
problem_bank.silver_description: Rearrange the equation, or use the power balance Vp Ip = Vs Is, before substituting.
problem_bank.gold_description: Two steps chained: find a voltage or current first, then efficiency or grid power loss.

steps.label: Step 1: Write the turns ratio equation

worked_examples.question: A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.
A transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary voltage of 11.5 V. The secondary current is 4 A. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate the primary current.
A transformer steps down from 240 V to 12 V. The secondary current is 4 A and the primary current is 0.25 A. Calculate the efficiency of the transformer.

bronze.title: Bronze: one transformer equation
steps: The turns ratio links voltage and turns: \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\). More secondary turns steps the voltage UP; fewer steps it DOWN.
Rearrange for the unknown, then substitute. To find a secondary voltage: \(V_s = V_p \times \frac{n_s}{n_p}\).
Check: your voltage ratio should equal your turns ratio.

example.question: A transformer has 800 primary turns and 200 secondary turns. The primary voltage is 240 V. Find the secondary voltage.

steps.label: Check
steps.content: \(60 \div 240 = 0.25\), the same as the turns ratio ✓

silver.title: Silver: rearrange, or use power balance
steps: Sometimes you must rearrange the turns ratio first, for example \(n_s = n_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}\).
For currents, a 100% efficient transformer obeys power in = power out: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\). The low-voltage side carries the higher current.
Pick the equation that already contains three of your four quantities, then solve for the fourth.

example.question: A transformer has Vp = 230 V, Ip = 0.5 A and Vs = 46 V. Find Is (100% efficient).

gold.title: Gold: two steps chained
steps: Gold questions need two equations. You might find a voltage from the turns ratio, then a current from \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\).
Grid questions use power loss \(= I^2 R\). Because current is squared, transmitting at high voltage (small current) cuts the heating loss sharply.

example.question: 230 V and Ip = 2 A go into a transformer that is 80% efficient. Find the power output.

opener.label: Before any physics
opener.display:
A bike in low gear: you pedal fast but the wheel pushes hard and turns slowly.
In high gear: the wheel spins fast but pushes gently.
The power you put in comes straight out either way.

steps.say: No physics yet. Suppose you pedal in 100 watts of power. In a perfect gear system, how many watts come out at the wheel?
steps.hint: A gear trades speed for force, but it cannot create energy. What goes in comes out.

steps.say: Exactly. A gear trades speed for force but keeps the power the same. A transformer does the identical trick with electricity: it trades voltage for current, keeping power the same.
steps.pre: So if a transformer takes in 12 W, how many watts come out (100% efficient)?
steps.hint: Same rule: power in = power out.

steps.say: That is the whole idea: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\), power in equals power out. Step the voltage UP and the current must come DOWN to keep the product the same. The turns ratio \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\) sets how big the trade is.

bronze.display: A transformer steps 230 V down to 46 V. The primary coil has 1500 turns. Find the number of secondary turns.
bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: Turns and voltages share the same ratio: \(n_s = n_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}\).

steps.hint: Divide the secondary voltage by the primary voltage.

steps.say: Fewer secondary turns, exactly as you would expect for a step-down.
steps.hint: Multiply the primary turns by the voltage fraction.
Divide the primary turns by your answer.
Divide the primary voltage by the secondary voltage.
steps.done: Turns ratio 5 = voltage ratio 5, so ns = 300 turns.

silver.display: A step-down transformer has 2000 primary turns, 100 secondary turns, a primary voltage of 230 V and a secondary current of 8 A. Find the primary current (100% efficient).
silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: Two moves: the turns ratio gives Vs, then power balance \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) gives Ip.

steps.hint: Multiply the primary voltage by the turns ratio.

steps.say: Power in equals power out, so the primary carries this same 92 W.
steps.hint: Multiply the secondary voltage by the secondary current.

steps.say: Small primary current, big secondary current: that is step-down.
steps.hint: Divide the power by the primary voltage.
Multiply the primary voltage by your answer.
steps.done: Equals the secondary power 92 W, so Ip = 0.4 A.

gold.display: A generator produces 20 MW at 20,000 V. The cables have a total resistance of 5 Ω. Find the power lost in the cables, in MW.
gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: Find the current with \(I = \frac{P}{V}\), then the heating loss \(= I^2 R\). Convert MW to W first.
Current squared: the key to why the grid uses high voltage.
steps.hint: Square the current before multiplying by resistance.

steps.done: 5 MW lost out of 20 MW generated, so the answer is 5 MW.
